Wrist drop results from an inability to flex the wrist. It is often associated with radial nerve damage (as it supplies both muscles responsible for flexion of the wrist). The radial nerve also innervates the lateral side of the forearm (between the middle and little fingers) so a loss of sensation here would be expected. The radial nerve originates from the brachioradialis muscle which lies deep to the pronator teres muscle. Therefore if there was damage to the radial nerve via trauma or compression, the brachioradialis muscle will not receive innervation from the radial nerve. This means that this muscle will atrophy and the pronator teres muscle will pull the hand into the anatomical position - causing wrist drop. Damage to the ulnar nerve would result in claw hand as the muscles of the hand are unable to grip objects. The muscles of the forearm are still able to flex the wrist but the palmar interossei muscles are paralysed and therefore the hand is held in the claw position.  Sensory loss can be caused by damage to any nerve. The median nerve innervates the anterior/lateral side of the forearm (between the index finger and thumb). The ulnar nerve innervates the posterior/medial side of the forearm (between the little finger and middle finger). The radial nerve innervates the lateral side of the forearm between the middle finger and little finger. The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the anterior arm and chest. The medial pectoral nerve innervates the upper medial arm. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is secreted by the atria in response to high blood volume/pressure. It acts on the kidney and opposes the actions of aldosterone. Aldosterone stimulates the reabsorption of sodium in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct which increases blood pressure as more water is also reabsorbed. ANP reduces this effect by reducing sodium reabsorption. This reduces blood osmotic pressure and therefore reduces blood volume/pressure. It also causes the secretion of prostaglandin which causes vasodilation, further reducing blood pressure. ANP also has a negative feedback mechanism. If the blood pressure is high then more ANP will be released which will oppose aldosterone, if the blood pressure is low then less ANP will be released. This is part of the short-term regulation of blood pressure.  ADH is only involved with water reabsorption not sodium. Dendritic cells are a type of antigen-presenting cell that play a vital role in the adaptive immune response. They have the ability to migrate from the site of infection to draining lymph nodes where they can present MHC/peptide complexes to naïve T cells. This property means they are more effective at inducing an adaptive immune response than macrophages, which remain fixed in place.  Macrophages also have many similarities with dendritic cells. Both are found in peripheral tissues and both can present MHC/peptide complexes to T cells. However, unlike dendritic cells, macrophages cannot migrate to the lymph nodes. This prevents them from directly interacting with naïve T cells, meaning their capacity to induce an adaptive immune response is limited.  Macrophage function includes phagocytosis - the process by which foreign pathogens or material is engulfed and destroyed. Phagocytes recognize antigens on the surface of invading microorganisms through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). PRRs detect molecular patterns associated with microbial pathogens, such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria. Once phagocytosis has occurred, the contents of the cell are digested and processed into smaller peptide fragments which bind to class I MHC molecules inside the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). These peptides then travel to the cell membrane where they associate with MHCII proteins on its surface. This allows them to be recognized by T cells when they enter the draining lymph node.  Dendritic cells play an important role in activating naïve T cells, but once activated these cells become memory cells that can respond quickly if there's another infection. Without dendritic cells we wouldn't be able to mount an efficient adaptive immune response against pathogens.  In summary, while both macrophages and dendritic cells play important roles in innate immunity, it is the ability of dendritic cells to migrate to draining lymph nodes that makes them so effective at inducing an adaptive immune response. Failure of neural tube closure results in spina bifida - a condition where the vertebrae and connective tissue surrounding the spinal cord are formed normally but the spinal cord and its coverings may protrude through the skull or abdomen.  The hairy patch found on the newborn's back is a result of the neural tube failing to close at some point during embryonic development.  The cause of most cases of spina bifida is unknown.  There are two main types of spina bifida - Spina bifida occulta and Meningocele. Occulta refers to the term 'hidden' as the defect is usually covered by a piece of skin and hence hidden from view. The meningocele type occurs when the spinal cord and nerves develop normally, but the surrounding coverings (meninges) push out through the backbone to form a sac. This type of spina bifida is associated with mild to severe learning difficulties, bladder problems and weak leg muscles.  The third type is myelodysplasia (also known as Chiari II malformation). In this type of spina bifida, the spinal cord and nerves do not properly develop. This causes a range of disabling conditions such as paralysis, loss of sensation, incontinence and difficulty breathing. The barrier between the CNS & the rest of the body is called the blood-brain barrier. It's made up of endothelial cells (the same as those in blood vessels) but ependymal cells also contribute by secreting cerebrospinal fluid which bathes the CNS. This barrier has a lot of implications - it stops immune cells entering the brain so they can't deal with pathogens or damaged neurones, which is why meningitis is so dangerous. The correct answer is A - quinolones. These drugs block the action of the enzyme topoisomerase II which unlinks supercoiling in bacterial DNA before replication. This prevents the bacteria from completing replication, leading to cell death. Beta-lactams are a common type of antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections. However, they prevent the formation of cross links in the peptidoglycan layer of bacterial cells rather than affecting DNA replication. Tetracyclines bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit of bacteria, preventing protein synthesis and therefore killing the bacteria. Macrolides are a type of antibiotic that prevent the translation of bacterial RNA, again by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit. Aminoglycosides inhibit the formation of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence on bacterial mRNA, meaning it cannot be translated into proteins. Source: 'Molecular Genetics' lecture in Case 10. The ilioinguinal nerve supplies sensation to the root and anterior parts of the pubis and lower abdomen. It also supplies the skin covering the root and front of the scrotum in males.The ilioinguinal nerve innervates the cremaster muscle, which tenses when this nerve is stimulated (cremasteric reflex). This reflex is often used to check for nerve damage during surgery on the groin or upper thigh. The ilioinguinal nerve originates from the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and forms from the anterior primary divisions of the first two lumbar ventral rami. These branches are called the genital branch and the inferior genital branch. The genital branch runs medially along the deep inguinal ring to form a loop around the spermatic cord in males. In females, it passes through the inguinal canal to enter the labium majus. The inferior genital branch descends through the deep inguinal ring in males and enters the scrotum. The ilioinguinal nerve ends by dividing into multiple articular branches that run superficially over the testes and along the spermatic cord. It ends as these branches pass through the tunica vaginalis into the scrotum. The ilioinguinal nerve anastomoses with the genitofemoral nerve in the region of the deep inguinal ring.This nerve may be damaged during surgery to remove lymph nodes in the groin, such as during a radical inguinal orchiectomy. Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve may result in loss of sensation in the root and front of the scrotum and cause erectile dysfunction in men. The cremaster reflex (also known as the cremasteric reflex) is a reflex involving the cremaster muscle, which tenses when the ilioinguinal nerve is stimulated. The cremaster muscle lies within the inguinal canal in males; it extends from the internal oblique muscle of the abdomen to the superior aspect of the testicle(s), and is covered by the cremasteric fascia. When the ilioinguinal nerve is stimulated, the cremaster muscle contracts, causing the testicle(s) to rise and rotate towards the inguinal canal

90% of people are genetic carriers of the faulty CF gene. Symptoms include salt sweat, frequent chest infections and male infertility. The CF transmembrane regulator (CFTR) facilitates the diffusion of Cl- out of cells which causes water to follow, resulting in 'salt sweat'. The faulty CFTR does not allow Cl- out of cells so water cannot leave either, resulting in very thick mucus on the epithelium which is easy prey for bacteria. The faulty CFTR also results in poor sperm motility as they need a watery environment to swim in. Foramen ovale closure: After the first breath, O2 enters the alveoli for the first time and it signals the arterioles to dilate. This sudden dilation leads to a large drop in pressure in the pulmonary system. Pressure in the right atrium is now significantly lower than in the left atrium. A pressure gradient is established from left to right which forces blood through the foramen ovale into the left atrium. The muscle walls of the septum primum and septum secundum are pushed outwards as they fill with blood. They cannot close off the opening completely as there is still some blood flowing through them. However, the force of the blood moving through the hole is enough to push the valves shut, so that the only way the blood can pass to the right side is via the lungs.  http://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor69  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor72  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor73  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor85  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor88  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor91  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%20Foetal%20Circulation.htm#anchor96  https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD014%2

Respiratory acidosis = PaO2 < 8.7kPa with pH < 7.35Respiratory alkalosis = PaO2 > 8.7kPa with pH > 7.35Metabolic acidosis = pH < 7.35 with plasma HCO3- less than 22Metabolic alkalosis = pH > 7.35 with plasma HCO3- greater than 22Compensation can be either way i.e. in response to a primary disturbance  Raised CO2 will cause respiratory alkalosis and lower HCO3- will cause metabolic acidosis.  Decreased CO2 will cause respiratory acidosis and raised HCO3- will cause metabolic alkalosis.  If there is no compensation then it is uncompensated.   In this case the patient has respiratory acidosis with a low pH and a high PaCO2 so that is the primary disturbance.  The other variables are all abnormal but not as much as the PaO2 and pH so they are secondary responses.  The high PaCO2 has caused a rise in HCO3- which may be trying to compensate for the acidosis.  The low pO2 has caused a rise in pH which is causing the alkalosis.  Therefore the answer is option B.  The fact that the patient has a long history of COPD means that this is likely to be chronic respiratory acidosis where the body is unable to fully compensate.  This is because you cannot get rid of CO2 completely and you cannot increase HCO3- levels too much. Vitamin A is required for rhodopsin synthesis which allows us to see in low light conditions. Excessive vitamin E intake interferes with vitamin A absorption. Low levels of vitamin A will result in poor vision in low light. Vitamin A deficiency can lead to night blindness. Rhodopsin is a protein found in rod cells which allows them to convert from a hydrophobic to hydrophilic form when exposed to light. This enables them to activate ion channels so that the electrical impulse can be generated. Vitamin E does not have any known link to night blindness. However, it does protect cell membranes from free radicals.Vitamins B5, B12 and K are all important components of methylation. Methylation is essential in the synthesis of Coenzyme A (CoA), which is required for the first step of the Kreb's Cycle. Low levels of these vitamins will prevent the formation of CoA and therefore prevent the oxidation of carbohydrates and fats. Vitamin D is used in the synthesis of calcitriol, which is a hormone involved in calcium absorption. It also plays a role in regulating phosphate levels. An excess of vitamin E would not affect calcium absorption as there are other hormones involved which regulate calcium absorption. Vitamin E is an antioxidant and is important in protecting cell membranes from free radicals.
